title: Lesson 1: The Vertex Form of a Quadratic Function
central_question: If you only have the equation of a curve that rises and then falls (or the other way around), how do you know where the high or low point is — and how do you know a rewritten equation is still the same curve?
intended_understanding: A quadratic written as f(x) = a(x − h)^2 + k makes the vertex (h, k), the axis of symmetry, and the maximum or minimum readable from the equation; changing a, h, or k moves the graph in a way students can predict and then check. Expanding that vertex-form equation produces an equivalent standard form, which graphing technology confirms as the same curve, not a new one.
prerequisite_assumptions: Students can evaluate f(x) in function notation, so they can talk about the vertex as the point where f(h) = k (Module 1 Lesson 3; A2.2).

Roles of a, h, and k as transformations of y = x^2 are already taught (Module 1 Lesson 4; A2.5). This lesson reuses that language to read vertex form; it does not reteach stretching, reflecting, or sliding.
Students can already sketch g(x) = a(x − h)^2 + k from y = x^2 (Module 1 Lessons 5–6; A2.6).
Students already know that the vertex is a maximum or a minimum that bounds the range (Module 1 Lesson 7; A2.3).
Students can expand and simplify quadratic expressions, including binomial squares, so they can expand a(x − h)^2 + k (Module 2 Lessons 1–2; A1.2).
Students have already inspected standard form and factored form for intercepts and related features (Module 3; A2.10 share). This lesson adds vertex-form inspection to that three-form comparison.
Students have already located a vertex from x-intercepts in factored form (A2.9), so vertex form is a second way to see the same point.
processes_to_teach: Inspect vertex form f(x) = a(x − h)^2 + k: name the vertex (h, k) including plus-inside (x + …), the axis of symmetry x = h, and whether the vertex is a maximum or a minimum from the sign of a (not from k or the quadrant). Full fade: worked → variation → partial → independent → retrieval.

Expand f(x) = a(x − h)^2 + k into f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c and verify, using graphing technology, that the two writings are equivalent representations. Full fade: worked → variation → partial → independent → retrieval.

Describe what can be read from vertex form compared with standard form and factored form, and defend vertex form when the decision is the high or low point, without producing those other writings. Full fade (compact: the contrast is conceptual, not a new algorithm).

Find zeros of a given vertex-form equation by inverse operations only (no quadratic formula, no completing the square). Compact full fade. Supports A2.10’s intercepts example; intercepts are not readable by inspection the way they are from factored form.

Construct a vertex-form equation from a vertex plus another point (or from stated constraints), and say what remains free if only the vertex is known. Compact full fade. Occupies families vertex-and-point-to-function and constraint-construction.

Predict from the equation what changing one of a, h, or k will do to the graph, then check that prediction against the graph and the rewritten equation (one parameter at a time). Interactive already teaches predict/check on the vertex board. Do not add a second paper fade. Pool family predict-parameter-change lives in that Action beat only.

process_fade.note: Partial slot is student error-diagnosis (h-sign, max-from-k), not a third identical reading. Axis claim-testing is independent/transfer of this process.
Partial slot is the expansion error-diagnosis item. Method-choice (prove for all x) and table claim-testing are transfer of this process, not extra expand drills.
Worked contrast, then students defend a form for a stated decision (form-affordances method-choice item).
Inverse operations only. The zeros method-choice item is variation/transfer, not a formula lesson.
Worked: recover a from vertex and a point. Variation: graph/table features mapped to a, h, k. Partial/independent: same vertex different a; vertex-only degrees of freedom.
Vertex-board predict → move one parameter → submit → check. No duplicate paper sequence.

purpose_map.purpose: Put students in a situation where the high or low point of a quadratic model is the thing they need, before any reminder that they already know transformations of y = x^2. Pool family: maximum-from-representations (situation only; do not solve the later retrieval item here).
Have students commit to a vertex from a plus-inside vertex-form equation so the h-sign reading is visible before they use the graph. Pool family: read-vertex-features (diagnostic).
Fully demonstrate how to read vertex, axis, and maximum or minimum from one vertex-form equation, including matching (x + …) to (x − h). Pool family: read-vertex-features (worked).
Repeat that reading on a second equation that varies the sign of a or uses k = 0, so maximum versus minimum cannot be taken from k. Pool family: read-vertex-features (variation).

Students locate and repair a first invalid step in someone else’s vertex reading (h-sign; maximum from the sign of k), then prove, qualify, or refute the claim that the axis is y = h. Assembled student work, not drawer-only. Pool families: error-diagnosis (inspection errors); claim-testing (axis). This is the partial-to-independent work for inspect-vertex-form.

Students predict a graph and equation change from altering one parameter, move that parameter, submit evidence, and explain what the graph and equation now say. The board already teaches predict/check — do not add a paper fade. Keep the consolidation fresh-case graph out of this beat. Pool family: predict-parameter-change.

Students expand vertex form into standard form themselves, then use graphing technology to confirm the two writings are the same parabola. Full fade of equivalent-forms (worked, variation, then independent ministry expand). Pool family: equivalent-forms.

purpose_map.section: action: method-choice, table claim, expand error
purpose_map.purpose: Students choose algebra versus a graph under the criterion “prove they are the same function for every x,” refute the claim that matching table values prove identity, and repair a first invalid expansion step. Assembled student work, not drawer-only. Pool families: method-choice; claim-testing (table-as-proof); error-diagnosis (expand). Transfer and partial slots for expand-and-verify.

Name what vertex form makes readable compared with standard and factored form, then defend a form for a stated decision (highest point, not intercepts), without asking students to produce those other writings. Pool family: form-affordances.

From a given vertex-form equation, find zeros by undoing operations (both signs); then choose a method under “exact values with the least extra algebra.” No quadratic formula. Pool family: zeros-from-vertex-form (includes its method-choice item).

Students write a vertex-form equation from a vertex and another point (or from a labelled graph/table), construct two different writings with the same vertex, and say what is still free if only the vertex is known. Assembled student work, not drawer-only. Pool families: vertex-and-point-to-function; constraint-construction; representation-bridge.

Return to the hook situation with a fresh vertex-form equation: read vertex, axis, and maximum or minimum independently; retrieve that expanding the writing does not move the curve; read a maximum from a given vertex-form model; judge a meaningful domain for that given model (not a full applications lesson). Pool families: read-vertex-features (retrieval); equivalent-forms (retrieval); maximum-from-representations (retrieval); model-critique (assembled once; not A3.3).

drawer_policy: Parent maps fade cells to accepted vf-* ids. Extra accepted items in an assembled family may remain in the drawer after those cells are filled. Excluded records (Nelson bank, MathNet 0gz2, regression) stay out of the student page. data-modelling is drawer-only.
solution_convention: Word-problem solutions (maximum-from-representations, model-critique, hook return) use Search / Translate / Answer / Review plus a supporting diagram. That structure is for authored solutions only. Do not put STAR labels, or Situation/Task/Action/Result, into student-facing copy in this brief or later stems.
hook_constraint: Need a situation where the high or low point of a quadratic model is the decision students care about (path, throw, fountain, height, and similar). The lesson must return to that same situation in consolidation. Do not open by reminding students that they already know stretching, flipping, or sliding y = x^2. A fountain or water-arc image is allowed only if a reusable signed-out source exists; otherwise use a situation that needs no photo. No required login, Gizmos, or Desmos API.
instructional_sequence_intent: Need the high or low point from an equation (hook, family maximum-from-representations) → plus-inside diagnostic (read-vertex-features) → worked then varied inspection → student error-diagnosis and axis claim-testing → predict/move/check on the board only (predict-parameter-change) → expand fade (equivalent-forms) → method-choice, table claim-testing, expand error-diagnosis → form-affordances → zeros by inverse operations → construct from constraints (vertex-and-point, constraint-construction, representation-bridge) → consolidation retrieval on the hook equation plus light model-critique.

expectations.statement: express the equation of a quadratic function in the standard form f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c, given the vertex form f(x) = a(x − h)^2 + k, and verify, using graphing technology, that these forms are equivalent representations
expectations.sample_problem: Given the vertex form f(x) = 3(x − 1)^2 + 4, express the equation in standard form. Use technology to compare the graphs of these two forms of the equation.
expectations.why_this_lesson: The named lesson starts from vertex form. Expanding to standard form and checking graphs is the algebraic identity of that form, without completing the square.

expectations.statement: describe the information (e.g., maximum, intercepts) that can be obtained by inspecting the standard form f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c, the vertex form f(x) = a(x − h)^2 + k, and the factored form f(x) = a(x − r)(x − s) of a quadratic function
expectations.why_this_lesson: This lesson addresses inspecting vertex form for vertex, maximum or minimum, and axis. The Ministry statement also names standard and factored form; those inspection shares were Module 3 (strand-map note: A2.10 spans M3 and M4).

misconceptions.label: instructional_hypothesis
misconceptions.hypothesis: Students take the vertex as (−h, k) or (h, k) by looking at the written sign instead of reading (x − h), so f(x) = (x + 3)^2 + 1 is placed at (3, 1) or they always negate every number they see.

misconceptions.label: instructional_hypothesis
misconceptions.hypothesis: Students swap the roles of a and k: a stretch or reflection is described as a vertical shift, or k is treated as a stretch factor.

misconceptions.label: instructional_hypothesis
misconceptions.hypothesis: Students think expanding vertex form into standard form produces a different parabola rather than an equivalent representation.

misconceptions.label: instructional_hypothesis
misconceptions.hypothesis: Students expect x-intercepts to be as immediately readable from vertex form as they are from factored form, or they treat (h, k) as an intercept.

misconceptions.label: instructional_hypothesis
misconceptions.hypothesis: Students write the axis of symmetry as y = h (or y = k) instead of x = h.

misconceptions.label: instructional_hypothesis
misconceptions.hypothesis: Students decide maximum versus minimum from the sign of k, or from whether the vertex is in quadrant I, instead of from the sign of a.

misconceptions.label: instructional_hypothesis
misconceptions.hypothesis: Students treat a few matching table values or a graphing-window overlap as a proof that two writings are the same function for every x.
